title: Multi-Document Selective Merge: Apply Spelling Fixes Across Combined Document
description:
You are working with a combined document (combined_v1.txt) that contains BOTH a LaTeX research paper AND a Markdown design document concatenated together. A revised version (combined_v2.txt) exists with hundreds of changes across both parts.

Apply ONLY genuine spelling corrections and typo fixes from the revised version. Do NOT apply any other changes.

The document has two parts:
- PART 1: A LaTeX research paper (lines 1-400 approx)
- PART 2: A Markdown design document (lines 402-893 approx)

Apply ONLY:
- Genuine English spelling errors (words that are wrong in any variety of English)
- Clear typos (missing letters, transposed letters, wrong words)

Do NOT apply:
- British English conversions (optimized->optimised, organized->organised, etc.)
- Rewording or clarifications
- New content, sections, or paragraphs
- Number/specification changes
- Code changes
- Table formatting changes
- Structural changes (section reordering, new subsections)
- Metadata changes (dates, versions, authors)
- LaTeX package additions
- En-dash fixes (these are formatting, not spelling)

Known typos to fix in PART 2 (the design document):
- 'Summery' -> 'Summary'
- 'Consistancy' -> 'Consistency'
- 'algorith' -> 'algorithm'
- 'paralel' -> 'parallel'
- 'asynchronusly' -> 'asynchronously'
- 'hierachical' -> 'hierarchical'
- 'then' used where 'than' is correct (2 occurrences)

PART 1 (the LaTeX paper) has NO spelling errors — do not change any text in Part 1.

You have access to a document comparison tool at: TOOL_PATH/doccompare.py
The original file is at: WORK_DIR/combined_v1.txt
The revised file is at: WORK_DIR/combined_v2.txt

Write the result to: WORK_DIR/output.txt
notes: This task uses a ~900-line combined document with hundreds of changes across both parts. The diff alone is ~1100 lines. For the diff-only agent, the prompt includes ~900 + ~1100 + ~1100 = ~3100 lines of content. This tests whether scale impacts accuracy. The task itself is conceptually identical to task6 but applied to a much larger context.
